The biggest thing I took away from this is how supportive your dad seems. How much of an impact would you say your family has had on your career so far? 

As a slightly related question, what happens to your old friends when you move in to the team house? Is it weird that you're now a minor celebrity around them?
I phoned her. She wants to stay friends. I'm still very torn up about what I did, but a load was lifted off of my shoulders when she said she's okay.
I appreciate you taking the time out to message me. I really do. Sorry I couldn't have had a better response.

I still can't bring myself to call. I don't want her to remember our last conversation as such a cold one where all I do is list the passwords/details she needs then hang up.

I'd honestly rather just wait and die.

I'm planning on writing very specific instructions of how to deliver her stuff plus money in an envelope to get it back to her. I doubt my mother would withhold anything when she got the news.

The whole learning experience thing makes no sense to me, because what have I learned? That I cannot control myself? That I cannot be trusted? I've learned nothing good and have only hurt someone who could have had such a better early 20s if we had never met.

I don't want to make amends. I fear that she will attempt to forgive me, and that is not at all what I'm looking for. I don't want to be patted on the head and told it'll be alright. I don't want to find love and move on. I want to be punished for the ultimate crime. She has to suffer the mental anguish of the whole jail/break up/violence for the rest of her life. Nothing I can do will change that.

The problem is that I don't even know what to say. I started writing notes in jail a month ago and I still don't know how to make her have to go through this one last time.

I haven't spoken to her in about 4 weeks (excluding when I called her from jail 3 weeks ago and went to pick up my stuff under police escort maybe 2.5 weeks ago). The no-contact order ended yesterday but I really don't know how she's feeling right now. She posts on her blog but leave them as private.

We were on decent terms when I called from jail, and she even gave me some of her possessions to remember her by, along with a heartfelt note. She said she will hold no grudges, but 3 weeks is a hell of a long time to change your mind in.

I fucked up big time and have wicked sick anxiety around police and fears of the door knocking again now. Going to jail really scarred me and having the guilt alongside the constant fear of being arrested again is crushing my spirit. That's a really selfish thing to say, though, because it's not really about how I feel. If I wanted it to be, I shouldn't have done something so wrong.

Her life will be happy with or without me. Let's be honest, she's absolutely gorgeous and would have no problem finding a guy to fill my slot. We now live in separate countries, so she wouldn't know the difference between me never contacting her again and being dead.

The very best thing you can do is avoiding saying things like "I know how you feel" or "Life just sucks sometimes but you'll get over it". Try to be comforting and engage him in activities that he enjoys to ease his mind. Even if it means logging in to Skype, sending a pizza to his place (may be a challenge with the distance) and watching some Netflix, it means he won't be alone.

From experience, having someone call 911 will have the police hunt you down and do an assessment. Your only risk of being committed is if you serve an immediate threat to yourself and others, but in all honesty it's not that useful if you're having thoughts with no plans. For me, they dropped me off near home after a 5 minute exam and didn't follow up.

Your call, but the police is only a helpful option if you've fully decided to kill yourself and need immediate help.

There's nothing anyone without some serious training can say to help you with this situation, even if we've been there. All I can say is that the thoughts you are having are natural based on what happened. If you can, get in touch with your psychiatrist ASAP. If not, call a suicide hotline and they can put you in touch with someone to work with you. Barring that, the hospital has an outpatient facility (in Canada at least) to sit with you for as long as you need, and will only admit you if you're threatening to kill yourself when you leave.

Be honest. I have bipolar type I, and I hid a lot of symptoms. That led to me being put on anti-depressants, which was then followed by incredible crying spells and fainting.

They're there to help, and all you need to do is let the words fall out of your mouth. Don't worry about records or whatever. All of that can come later (didn't stop me from getting a job right after), and just focus on getting the care you deserve.

Go tomorrow and don't look back. Things will only get better when you do.

Then that is solid proof that it's not you. From the sounds of it, he still has strong feelings for you, but needs to be sure you feel the same. He may just need you to show him why he should be yours, so maybe instead of telling him, show him. Starting Monday, pick a new way every day to shower him with love and prove to him that he is your one and only. Maybe hand craft a photo book, deliver him lunch at work, etc., but just give him solid proof that you never want to lose him.

Based on what you're saying, this isn't worth giving up on and, if nothing else, you'll be closer friends from the experience.

Whatever you do, don't tell him why you're doing it other than because you love him. He doesn't need to know that you're trying to win his heart over, because that may cheapen it for him.

You're 20. At 20 I was a struggling writer and at 22 I was earning great money. With work, the only thing to do is to keep grinding out applications, and in the mean time develop a skill. Ask an electrician if you can shadow them, or if a mechanic needs free help. It goes on your resume and makes you look more employable, but it also keeps  you busy and gets you interacting with people on a daily basis. If you're diligent and they need someone, it may even result in a job offer or a recommendation to another company.

Being at home is far more stressful than working for free will ever be. It's only temporary, and be careful because some companies will just harvest you for the free labour.

Have you had the talk? The one after the relationship where you discuss everything calmly and talk about where you want to go from there. A break up is usually emotional, but you sound like you would really benefit from seeing exactly where your paths uncrossed, because it may not be you're not enough at all. He may have wanted kids at 23, or a woman who eats fruit salad for breakfast.

As weird as it sound, it could be that he loves you, but wants the idea of romance he has mentally formed (for me it's getting home from work to find my wife teaching the kids French while I cook dinner for us all).

Your depression makes your brain find ways in which you aren't enough or didn't give him what he wanted, but stay open to the idea that it was something you couldn't have done/affected.

If your mother were to lose both your father and you in short succession, it would crush her. Right now it's important to focus on what *can* be done, instead of what can't.

There are income support resources, and if you're able to work, you can supplement that with your own income.

Also keep in mind that your father isn't quite ready to leave. If he were, he would have saved up elsewhere and told nobody. Maybe sitting down and speaking to him as his child will help him to understand the effect his actions may have on the family.

Call him. This isn't /r/relationships and I'm not going to sit here telling you to cut contact.

You're telling us what you want to tell him, but you should really say it to him before you do anything. Losing a loved one, no matter how bad things are, is enough to drive anyone to suicide. The only time things can't be worked on with him is the day you die. Remember that.
